overview: Nkore was one of the Great Lakes kingdoms in what is now southwestern Uganda. The imported 1815 to 1878 interval is a map window, not its lifespan. The outline extends far west into today’s Democratic Republic of the Congo and misses much of the Nkore heartland; it is not a reliable political boundary. Later Ankole institutions and museum objects are identified below by their own dates.

periods.title: The mapped precolonial kingdom
periods.summary: Nkore retained independence amid pressure from larger neighbours. Royal power and local authority were closely connected to cattle.

periods.title: A later colonial settlement
periods.summary: British supremacy replaced independent rule. Colonial Ankole incorporated additional territory and cannot simply be projected backward onto old Nkore.

periods.title: Monarchy within a larger state
periods.summary: The 1901 agreement preserved chiefs under colonial supervision. The monarchy continued through later political arrangements before abolition in 1967.

sections.title: Finding a kingdom beyond its outline

items.text: Nkore was smaller than Rwanda and Buganda but maintained political independence through repeated pressures and raids. Historian D. A. Low places its eventual submission to British domination between 1898 and 1901, after this map window closes. Its story is not a conquest dated to 1878.

In 1987, Andrew Reid and Peter Robertshaw revisited former capital sites linked in oral traditions to particular Bagabe, or rulers. They assessed places with potential for excavation. Matching remembered royal locations with surviving earth and settlement traces is a research method, not a license to invent a palace plan.

sections.title: Herds, homes and education in a later account

items.text: Writing in 1915, missionary John Roscoe described herders arranging temporary grass houses around a circle, with doors facing inward and thorn barriers between them. The enclosure kept cattle together at night. This later, partial outsider account records a practical settlement design, not every family’s house in 1815.

Roscoe also described clay watering troughs where cattle could not reach the water directly. Some people drew water while others controlled crowding so each animal could drink. Managing a herd meant planning the queue as well as finding the grass.

In Roscoe’s account, young princes were placed with responsible chiefs to learn cattle management and community customs. Royal training could include practical herding knowledge, not just ceremony. The account was published in 1915 and should not be treated as a school timetable for all children.

sections.title: Objects explained by a local museum

items.text: Igongo’s 2012 catalogue documents a churning gourd and a small clay pot used to scent milk containers with smoke. The latter fitted beneath an inverted vessel while fragrant herbs burned inside. These objects record skilled milk preparation; the catalogue does not date them to the map’s nineteenth-century interval.

A three-metre papyrus-and-reed stretcher, called engozi, is documented for carrying sick people, brides or the dead in Ankole and Kigezi. It shows how neighbours could transport someone without a wheeled vehicle: a practical piece of equipment with several very different community uses.

The catalogue’s gourd trumpet was played by herders to relieve boredom, including by imitating birds and cattle. Looking after a herd could have a soundtrack. The explanation comes from museum staff in March 2012, rather than an assumed ancient invention date.

“Enyungu y’amaizi” means “water pot” in the Runyankore label printed in that 2012 catalogue. Its clay vessel rests on a dry banana-fibre ring. This is attested modern writing in Latin script, paired with the museum’s English translation, rather than a surviving precolonial inscription.

sections.title: What colonial rule changed, and what survives

items.text: Under British rule, Ankole became larger even as its ruler lost independent sovereignty. Low describes Mbaguta emerging as its principal chief after rivals were removed. Political survival therefore included negotiation and unequal power, while the boundaries of the colonial kingdom differed from those of older Nkore.

The 1901 agreement recognized Kahaya and named chiefs but allowed British authorities to depose them for breaching its terms. It imposed hut and gun taxes and placed major land and mineral claims under colonial government. A written agreement could preserve titles while sharply restricting what their holders controlled.

A 2021 Cambridge museum report describes work with Uganda’s museum on returning selected objects on loan, including material representing Ankole and Bahima communities. It acknowledges varied acquisition routes, including confiscation, theft, gifts and purchases. Studying an object also means asking how it left its owners.

ending.text: The 1878 map endpoint did not end Nkore. Colonial rule changed its institutions around 1901, and Uganda abolished the monarchies in 1967 under Milton Obote. Abolishing a royal office did not erase Banyankore people, Runyankore or the knowledge preserved in families and museums. The older independent kingdom, colonial Ankole and living communities should remain distinct.
